first_run.title: Websites you own: a reply to an infographic that sells AI-built websites by the month, section by section, why rent is the wrong model, and the one-off model I propose, where the client owns Claude, GitHub and the domain, and changes their own site by talking to it

The Web Summit team, part five: the last day of setup, 180 releases, every person getting a key, an accountant counting the team's tokens, synthetic users testing the merch, and an inbox only the agents can write to

Spend fewer tokens: an agentic team's token bill is mostly a design choice, and the levers are files as memory, caching what repeats, code instead of models where you can, the right model for each step, no copy and paste, static outputs, and counting it all

The website cell: what we now sell, a GitHub repository fully set up with a live site on its own address, a CLAUDE.md and a behaviour policy, five designs by a team of agents, and then the site is yours to change with your own Claude, what it should cost, how it compares with Wix, Squarespace, Framer, Lovable and a freelancer, who already sells something close to it, and where to find buyers and partners

Sovereign websites, the investment case: PrompTugal's investor decks rewritten for a deliverable that is needed everywhere, in every language, in a market built on rent and lock-in, a one-off delivery that is already fully agentic, value given before payment through a demo in a vault, a long list of upsells, and why this is now a proper, scalable, investable architecture
Paying after the value: why a balance that can go negative feels different from a subscription, the psychology behind it, and the experiment this newsroom is running
sgit in GitHub Actions, side by side: a showcase repository and site that runs four ways of moving a vault between jobs on every run, measured, with a budget for its LLM steps
The tokens hook: a token behaviour policy that shows what every session reads, caches, writes and costs, why a prompt cannot do it, and a brief for tokens.hook.sgit.ai

Selling mini agentic teams: a business that sets up small agentic teams for companies, sized from one agent to a network, with a control centre to see them and to start and stop them, PrompTugal as the first customer and Agent Behaviour Policies as the most demanding version

Pennies against dollars: what our agents actually cost at Web Summit, the swarm that ran 216 model calls on four open-weight models for under seven cents where the same tokens on a frontier model would have cost about two dollars, newsroom days of hundreds of API-equivalent dollars, almost all of it agents re-reading their own sessions, and the lesson that context is the cost and starting again is cheaper than remembering
Agentics, ready to sell: what we showed at Agentic Engineering Live, who else is selling agentic services and at what price, the engagement path, and a marketplace for the consultants who deliver it

Specialist agents for every team: long-lived agents that keep one skill, design, UX, code, security, behaviour policies or writing, with a person who owns it, so that new teams start from our best work instead of from scratch, and why that makes expertise that never scaled into something you can hire, even from another company

Rent or own: Fliplet, an AI software builder advertised on the London Underground, against the AgentiCCells website cell, both building from a plain-language description and changing by talking to an AI, one a monthly platform paid in credits, the other a one-off build handed over into the customer's own repository, and why we should promise to move every site into its owner's hands within three months

Transcription for a sector, sold as a team: extending VoiceDebrief with what we have learnt from sovereign websites, a bundle for one industry, a repository the customer's own AI runs, with the whole pipeline from dropping a recording to a reviewed document and a team of agents certified by people from that sector, sold by small AI companies who know the industry, open source underneath, from £50 to £5,000
A custom Firefox of my own: the full plan to build one with a governed agent hive, for the laptop and the iPad, and how Mozilla could sell me the part I do not want to do, which is keeping it working

Inside Kitewing Websites: a made-up studio that sells websites you own, and three made-up client sites built as vault apps, a potter's catalogue, a community garden and a local plumber's guides library, each one file, each different, and each ready to be changed by talking to it
secrets.sgit.ai on public keys: no more shared keys, eight ways a secret moves, a vault for the private key, and the commercial service it becomes
Research, delivered as a vault: what companies that sell research could do with fractal graphs, behaviour policies for AI-enabled products, and evaluations run by a governed agent hive

Keys after payment: how to hand vault keys and access keys to customers once they have paid, what Stripe does and does not do after the money is taken, what FastSpring, Paddle, Lemon Squeezy, Polar, Gumroad and Square offer instead, and a design where the key is sealed to the buyer's own public key, keys are stock, and a payment provider can sell them without ever holding one

Paying the sources: the business model behind PrompTugal.news's data, a reader's money flowing back to the sources the reader actually read, worked out in the open and simulated for now, a licence link on every value, a public register of who we read and who we do not, and why a platform built on public data with no lock-in can be a positive loop for everyone who feeds it

The pitch: a site that looks better, that you own, that nobody can lock you into, that has almost nothing to attack, that costs once instead of every month, and that you change by talking to Claude, six promises, the proof behind each, and three designs for a site built on nothing else, "six promises", "just say it" and "stop renting your website"

Watch your website being built: a brief for a page that builds a first version of a sovereign website in the visitor's own browser, from a description or a voice note, with their own model key, showing every agent at work, every behaviour policy being applied and every penny it costs, then hands back a zip, the same brief run on several models side by side as evals, and the Web Summit demos it grows from

Websites for the moment: an experiment in letting an agent team keep building topical sites, around what people are looking for now, GTA VI on its launch day, Christmas posting dates, an advent of tools, the Kickstarter itself, each built in a day within a budget, every fact sourced, live for its moment and then archived, and a first calendar to start from
Knowledge that maintains itself: semantic graphs for an organisation's policies and internal knowledge, briefing people and agents from the graph, and vaults to carry the brief
The value of constraints: what client-side encryption and open source actually gave us, which is not what you would think
